opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a really important worry, and it's one we take seriously. When you say you want AI systems to be good at cooperation, you have to ask: cooperation with whom, and for what? The same capabilities that let agents find mutually beneficial agreements, like understanding each other, making credible commitments, and building trust, can also let them coordinate against the interests of others. Cartels are a form of cooperation. Collusion among firms setting prices is cooperation. So cooperative skill is, in that sense, dual-use.

But a few things push me toward thinking the research is still very much worth doing.

First, the baseline matters. If we don't invest in cooperative intelligence, we're not going to get a world without powerful AI agents interacting with each other. We'll get a world full of them, deployed by different actors with different goals, interacting at speeds and scales humans can't supervise in real time. Without deliberate work on cooperation, the default failure modes look like conflict, escalation, races to the bottom, and miscoordination. Those could be catastrophic. Many of the biggest risks we worry about, such as arms races, failures of bargaining that lead to war, and the tragedy of the commons on a global scale, are fundamentally cooperation failures.

Second, collusion is itself a cooperation problem that cooperative AI research helps us understand. To detect, prevent, or design against harmful collusion, you need a good theory of how agents come to coordinate, what makes commitments credible, and what signals they use. The field of Cooperative AI includes understanding when cooperation is socially desirable versus harmful, and designing institutions and mechanisms so that the cooperation we get is the broadly beneficial kind. Economists have long studied collusion precisely so that antitrust can work. We need the analogous science for AI.

Third, I'd distinguish between the narrow cooperation of a coalition and what you might call socially beneficial cooperation. A lot of what we're trying to promote isn't "make agents good at teaming up with each other," it's "make the overall system of humans and AIs better at achieving good outcomes for everyone." That includes norms, institutions, and accountability, where we're building cooperative capacity that's aligned with human welfare and embedded in governance structures, rather than raw coordination power floating free.

And finally, I think there's a meta-point: humanity's ability to navigate the transition to advanced AI depends heavily on our ability to cooperate, between labs, between countries, between AI developers and the public. AI tools that help humans understand each other, negotiate, and find common ground could be enormously valuable for that. Giving up on that whole space because some cooperative skills could be misused would be like refusing to study diplomacy because it could help conspirators.

So the honest answer is that there's a real tradeoff, and we should be thoughtful, prioritizing work that differentially advances beneficial cooperation and our ability to oversee and constrain collusion. But on balance, I think a world that understands cooperation deeply is much safer than one that doesn't.

r001.rationale: The response recommends prioritizing work that advances beneficial cooperation and helps constrain collusion, but it does not clearly call for judging whether individual components of the Cooperative AI research agenda are worth pursuing separately.

r002.rationale: It says humanity’s ability to navigate advanced AI depends on cooperation among labs, countries, developers, and the public, and that AI tools could help people negotiate and find common ground.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a really important question, and I want to be honest that collusion is a real concern. If you build systems that are better at modelling each other, communicating, making credible commitments, and coordinating, then in principle you've also built systems that are better at coordinating against humans, or against regulators, or against the firms and users they're supposed to be serving. That's a legitimate worry and I don't want to wave it away.

But I think when you look at it closely, a few things push me toward thinking the research is net positive, and actually quite strongly so.

The first is that cooperative capabilities are not really optional. The world is going to be full of AI systems interacting with each other — negotiating on behalf of people, managing supply chains, participating in markets, advising governments. Those interactions are going to happen whether or not anyone studies them carefully. And the default, if we don't think hard about it, is not "no cooperation." The default is that systems will stumble into whatever equilibria fall out of their training, which could include catastrophic failures of cooperation — escalation dynamics, commitment races, arms-race-type behaviour — as well as unintended collusion. So the choice isn't "cooperative AI versus a safe status quo." It's "understand these dynamics versus be surprised by them."

The second thing is that a lot of what we mean by Cooperative AI is really about understanding, not just capability. A big chunk of the agenda is about building the science: what are the conditions under which agents cooperate? How does communication change outcomes? When do commitment devices help and when do they hurt? What institutional structures make cooperation stable? If you understand that science, it also tells you how to detect and prevent collusion. The same theory that explains why two agents might coordinate on a cartel price also tells you what signals a regulator should look for, and what mechanism design choices make collusion harder. So I think the knowledge is fairly symmetric in a way that favours defence, because the defender — the human overseer — gets to set the rules of the game.

The third point, which I find quite compelling, is that the biggest risks from advanced AI probably aren't going to be solved purely at the level of individual system alignment. Even if you have systems that are each individually well-behaved, you can get terrible collective outcomes from the structure of their interactions. Think about climate change or nuclear arms races: those aren't failures of individual rationality, they're failures of collective action. I think the AI transition is going to generate a lot of problems that have that shape — between labs, between countries, between many deployed systems. If we want humanity to navigate that well, we need the tools to help humans cooperate, and AI that is good at facilitating cooperation might be one of the most important tools we have. That upside is large enough that I think it dominates.

And then finally, I'd say the practical answer to the collusion concern is to be deliberate about which capabilities you develop and how. Some of it is about differential progress — prioritising work on things like understanding, transparency, and verifiable commitment, which tend to help overseers more than they help colluders, and being more cautious about things like covert communication or deception-resistant coordination among agents. Some of it is about norms and governance within the research community. So I don't think the right response to the risk is "don't do the research." I think it's "do it thoughtfully, with the risk explicitly in view, and steer the portfolio toward the parts that empower human oversight."

So, on balance: real risk, but the alternative is worse, and the upside is potentially enormous.

r001.rationale: The response recommends choosing which capabilities to develop deliberately, prioritizing some areas and being more cautious about others. This communicates evaluating parts of the research agenda separately.

r002.rationale: The response argues that AI-related problems between labs, countries, and deployed systems require collective action, and that AI that helps humans cooperate could be an important tool.

astra-6.text:
I think the central reason is that failures of cooperation can be enormously costly. You can have actors who would all prefer some outcome, but who nevertheless end up in conflict because they can’t communicate clearly, make credible commitments, or trust one another. As AI systems become more capable and take on more consequential roles, we should want them to help resolve those problems.

But cooperation isn’t automatically good. Firms cooperating to fix prices are benefiting themselves at everyone else’s expense. And we certainly don’t want AI systems cooperating with one another to evade human oversight. So the objective can’t simply be to maximise cooperation among whichever agents happen to be interacting. We have to ask: cooperation between whom, toward what ends, and with what effects on other people?

That makes collusion an important research problem within cooperative AI. We want to understand what enables it, when it becomes harmful, and how to design systems and institutions that support beneficial cooperation while constraining harmful cooperation.

The alternative to pursuing this research isn’t necessarily a world where AI systems can’t collude. Those capabilities may emerge anyway as systems become better at planning and understanding each other. I’d rather we develop the understanding to distinguish desirable cooperation from collusion, and to steer these capabilities toward outcomes that are good for society.

r001.rationale: It asks which agents should cooperate and toward what ends, and treats collusion as a research problem, but does not call for evaluating individual components of the research agenda separately.

r002.rationale: It says failures of cooperation can be enormously costly and that increasingly capable AI systems should help resolve these problems, conveying that cooperation is important for good outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that we’re going to need AI systems to cooperate in order to get many of the benefits we want from them. We want them to help people reach agreements, avoid unnecessary conflict, and coordinate on shared problems. If we don’t understand how to make that work, we risk systems that are very capable individually but interact in ways that leave everyone worse off.

But the collusion concern is real. Cooperation among a particular group isn’t necessarily good for everyone else. Firms can cooperate to fix prices; systems could coordinate in ways that undermine human oversight. So the objective can’t simply be to maximise cooperation. We need to ask: cooperation between whom, towards what ends, and with what consequences for other people?

That’s part of why I think this is worth studying. We need to understand both how to enable beneficial cooperation and how to prevent harmful forms of it. Neglecting the research doesn’t make the possibility of collusion disappear; it could leave us less able to recognise and address it.

r001.rationale: The response supports studying beneficial cooperation and harmful collusion, but does not call for evaluating individual components of the research agenda separately.

r002.rationale: It says AI systems need to cooperate to help people coordinate on shared problems and achieve desired benefits, giving a reason to develop cooperative skills.
